title: Chapter 8 Drill: Breast, Endocrine Surgery, and Head and Neck

items.stem: A 61-year-old woman has a 1.4 cm area of grade 1 ductal carcinoma in situ on stereotactic biopsy, estrogen receptor positive, with calcifications confined to one quadrant and no mass. Clinical examination of the axilla is normal. She prefers to conserve her breast. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Lumpectomy alone with sentinel lymph node biopsy
Modified radical mastectomy with axillary node dissection
Lumpectomy with negative margins and whole-breast radiation, without axillary surgery
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by lumpectomy
items.explanation: Ductal carcinoma in situ by definition has not invaded the stroma, so it carries almost no risk of nodal metastasis, and axillary surgery is omitted when breast conservation is performed. Radiation lowers local recurrence after lumpectomy, and endocrine therapy may be offered for estrogen receptor positive disease. Axillary dissection and chemotherapy are unwarranted for noninvasive disease, and routine sentinel biopsy adds morbidity without benefit.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman finds a new 1.5 cm firm mass in the upper outer left breast. She is not pregnant or lactating and has no family history of cancer. Examination shows a discrete, mobile mass without skin change or adenopathy. Which imaging study should be obtained first?
options: Screening mammography of both breasts alone
Magnetic resonance imaging of both breasts with contrast and biopsy of any enhancing area
Positron emission tomography of the chest and axilla
Targeted breast ultrasound, with mammography added if findings are suspicious
items.explanation: In women under 30 with a palpable mass, ultrasound is the first study because dense breast tissue limits mammography and radiation exposure is avoided. Diagnostic mammography is added when ultrasound looks suspicious, and the triple assessment is completed with tissue sampling. Magnetic resonance imaging is not a first-line tool for a palpable mass, and positron emission tomography is not used to evaluate breast masses.

items.stem: After lumpectomy for a 1.6 cm invasive ductal carcinoma, the pathologist reports tumor cells at the inked margin of the specimen along the posterior surface. The sentinel node is negative. The patient still wishes to conserve her breast. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Whole-breast radiation with a boost and no further surgery
Re-excision to obtain a margin with no tumor at the ink
Completion mastectomy as the only acceptable choice
Axillary dissection to clear the margin status
items.explanation: For invasive cancer, the accepted standard after breast-conserving surgery is no tumor at the inked margin, and a positive margin is addressed by re-excision, or mastectomy if re-excision cannot achieve clearance or cosmesis. Radiation boost does not replace gross clearance. Mastectomy is not the only option when re-excision is feasible, and axillary surgery has no bearing on margin status.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has a 9 mm papillary thyroid carcinoma found incidentally on ultrasound for a carotid evaluation. Imaging shows no extrathyroidal extension, no suspicious nodes, and no adverse features. Which is an appropriate management option for this tumor?
options: Thyroid lobectomy, or active surveillance in selected low-risk patients
Total thyroidectomy with prophylactic central neck dissection and routine radioactive iodine
Bilateral modified radical neck dissection with thyroidectomy
External beam radiation to the thyroid bed alone
items.explanation: Low-risk papillary microcarcinoma has an excellent prognosis, and current guidelines allow lobectomy or active surveillance in selected patients, since more extensive surgery and radioactive iodine add risk without clear benefit. Prophylactic central dissection and bilateral dissection are overtreatment, and external beam radiation is reserved for aggressive or unresectable disease, not an incidental small papillary tumor.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman with a germline TP53 pathogenic variant is found to have a 1.8 cm invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast. She asks about breast conservation. Which operation is the best recommendation?
options: Lumpectomy followed by whole-breast radiation therapy
Bilateral mastectomy, to limit later radiation exposure in the chest
Lumpectomy with accelerated partial-breast irradiation
Unilateral mastectomy with no surveillance of the opposite breast afterward
items.explanation: Li-Fraumeni syndrome from a TP53 variant confers very high lifetime risks of breast cancer and other malignancies, and radiation therapy raises the risk of radiation-induced second cancers, so mastectomy is preferred and contralateral risk-reducing surgery is discussed. Breast conservation with any radiation form is therefore discouraged. Ignoring the other breast overlooks the high risk of a second primary cancer.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has a 3 cm cortisol-secreting right adrenal adenoma with suppressed ACTH. She undergoes laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Which perioperative step is most important to prevent a life-threatening complication?
options: Glucocorticoid coverage, then a taper guided by axis testing
Fludrocortisone alone, since mineralocorticoid is the missing hormone
No steroid, because the remaining gland recovers at once
A beta blocker started on the day of surgery
items.explanation: Chronic cortisol excess suppresses the contralateral adrenal and pituitary corticotrophs, so after removing the autonomous adenoma the patient is adrenally insufficient and needs perioperative glucocorticoid coverage, then a prolonged taper until the axis recovers on testing. Mineralocorticoid is not the problem since the renin axis is intact. Waiting for recovery risks adrenal crisis, and a beta blocker would not protect against it.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman has a rapidly enlarging 6 cm mobile breast mass. Core needle biopsy shows a cellular spindle-cell stroma with leaf-like architecture, moderate stromal atypia, and infiltrative borders, consistent with a borderline phyllodes tumor. Axillary examination is normal. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Enucleation of the mass with only a thin rim of normal tissue
Excision followed by routine axillary node dissection
Wide excision followed by adjuvant endocrine therapy
Wide local excision with a surgical margin of at least 1 cm
items.explanation: Phyllodes tumors are treated by wide local excision with margins of about 1 cm, or mastectomy when the mass is large relative to the breast. Enucleation leaves tumor at the edge and invites local recurrence. Phyllodes tumors spread by blood rather than lymphatics, so axillary dissection has no role. They are generally hormone receptor independent, so endocrine therapy adds nothing.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman has recurrent kidney stones, serum calcium of 11.4 mg/dL, and an elevated parathyroid hormone. Her mother had a pituitary tumor and her brother had a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. Genetic testing confirms a MEN1 variant. Which is the most appropriate operation for her hyperparathyroidism?
options: Focused excision of one gland localized by sestamibi scanning alone
Removal of the single largest gland and no exploration of the others
Subtotal parathyroidectomy with transcervical thymectomy
Total thyroidectomy with bilateral central neck dissection
items.explanation: In MEN1, hyperparathyroidism is multiglandular hyperplasia and is usually the first manifestation, so the operation is subtotal (three and a half gland) parathyroidectomy or total with autotransplantation, plus transcervical thymectomy to remove supernumerary and thymic rests. Focused or single-gland excision leaves hyperplastic glands that cause recurrence. The thyroid is not involved, so thyroidectomy has no role here.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man has serum calcium of 10.9 mg/dL with a normal parathyroid hormone level at the upper limit. His 24-hour urinary calcium excretion is very low, with a calcium to creatinine clearance ratio under 0.01. His father and daughter have mild hypercalcemia without symptoms. What is the best management?
options: Subtotal parathyroidectomy to prevent future kidney stones and bone loss
Cinacalcet therapy to target a normal serum calcium
Sestamibi scan to find a single adenoma for excision
Observation, since surgery does not correct this disorder
items.explanation: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia, usually from an inactivating calcium-sensing receptor variant, causes lifelong mild, asymptomatic hypercalcemia with low urine calcium and a ratio below 0.01. It is benign, and parathyroidectomy fails to correct it, so no treatment is needed. Imaging for an adenoma and subtotal surgery are pointless, and drug therapy aimed at normalizing calcium is unnecessary.

items.stem: During a right total thyroidectomy, the surgeon finds that the right inferior laryngeal nerve passes directly from the vagus to the larynx, without looping around a vessel. Which anatomic anomaly is most likely associated with this finding?
options: An aberrant right subclavian artery arising from the descending aorta
A right-sided aortic arch with mirror-image branching
A persistent thyroglossal duct tract remnant in the midline of the anterior neck
An absent right lobe of the thyroid gland
items.explanation: A nonrecurrent right inferior laryngeal nerve occurs when the right subclavian artery arises from the descending aorta as the last arch branch, so there is no fourth arch vessel for the nerve to loop around. It is encountered in roughly one percent of patients and is vulnerable because it enters the larynx at a different level and course. The other anomalies are not linked to this nerve variant.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman undergoes a right modified radical mastectomy for a 3.4 cm invasive ductal carcinoma. Final pathology shows metastases in five of fourteen axillary nodes, and the margins are negative. Which adjuvant local treatment is most appropriate?
options: No further local therapy because the surgical margins are clear and negative
Re-operation to remove the remaining axillary nodes
Chest wall and regional nodal radiation, along with systemic therapy
Radiation limited to the supraclavicular fossa alone
items.explanation: Four or more positive axillary nodes after mastectomy is a firm indication for postmastectomy radiation to the chest wall and regional nodes, which improves local control and survival. Negative margins alone do not remove this indication. Further surgery does not replace radiation, and treating only the supraclavicular fossa leaves the chest wall and other nodal basins untreated.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man who has smoked for decades has painless, slowly enlarging, soft masses in the tails of both parotid glands. Fine needle aspiration shows oncocytic epithelium with a lymphoid background. Technetium pertechnetate scanning shows increased uptake in both masses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma, the most common salivary cancer
Warthin tumor, a benign lesion that is often bilateral
Pleomorphic adenoma with early malignant transformation
Adenoid cystic carcinoma with perineural spread
items.explanation: Warthin tumor (papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum) occurs mainly in older men who smoke, favors the parotid tail, is often bilateral, shows oncocytes with lymphoid stroma, and takes up pertechnetate. It is benign and may be observed or excised. Pleomorphic adenoma is mixed epithelial and stromal, and mucoepidermoid and adenoid cystic carcinomas are malignant and do not give this pattern of uptake and cytology.

items.stem: A 27-year-old man has angioedema after a bee sting. He has stridor, drooling, and oxygen saturation of 78 percent. Epinephrine has been given, and orotracheal intubation attempts have failed twice with a view limited by swelling. Bag-mask ventilation is ineffective. What is the appropriate next step?
options: A third attempt at laryngoscopy with a different blade
Elective tracheostomy in the operating room
Emergency cricothyroidotomy through the cricothyroid membrane
Observation and nebulized steroid until swelling subsides
items.explanation: A cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate situation is an indication for an immediate surgical airway, and in an adult the cricothyroid membrane is the quickest, safest site for cricothyroidotomy, since it lies superficial and is easily found. Repeated laryngoscopy wastes time as saturations fall, and elective tracheostomy in an operating room takes longer than the patient can tolerate. Observation risks death.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a stereotactic core biopsy of a 7 mm cluster of fine calcifications. Pathology reports atypical ductal hyperplasia with no carcinoma. Calcifications are partly removed on the specimen radiograph, and the radiologist judges the findings concordant. Which is the best next step?
options: Annual mammography without further tissue sampling
Surgical excision to exclude an associated carcinoma
Bilateral prophylactic mastectomy to remove the risk
Radiation therapy to the involved quadrant of the breast
items.explanation: Atypical ductal hyperplasia on core biopsy is upgraded to ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive cancer in a meaningful fraction of cases at excision, so surgical excision is recommended. Imaging alone cannot exclude the upgrade. Prophylactic mastectomy is excessive for a single high-risk lesion, and radiation is a treatment for proven malignancy, not for a benign atypical lesion.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man of Southeast Asian descent has a painless right upper neck mass, serous otitis media, and nasal obstruction. Examination shows a 3 cm firm level V node. Which is the most appropriate step to establish the diagnosis?
options: Nasopharyngeal endoscopy with biopsy, and testing for Epstein-Barr virus
Open excisional biopsy of the neck node as the very first diagnostic procedure
Empiric antibiotics for two weeks, then reassessment
Total thyroidectomy with neck dissection of levels II to V
items.explanation: Unilateral serous otitis media and a posterior triangle node in an adult suggest nasopharyngeal carcinoma, which is associated with Epstein-Barr virus and is common in certain populations. Endoscopy with biopsy of the nasopharynx gives the diagnosis. Open node biopsy first can disrupt lymphatic drainage and complicate later neck treatment, antibiotics delay diagnosis, and surgery is not the primary treatment because this tumor is radiosensitive.

items.stem: A 4-year-old boy has a 2 cm smooth, midline neck mass just below the hyoid bone that rises when he protrudes his tongue. Ultrasound shows a thin-walled cyst, and a normal thyroid gland is visible in its usual position. Which operation is the appropriate treatment?
options: Simple cyst excision with preservation of the hyoid bone intact
Needle aspiration with injection of a sclerosing agent
Total thyroidectomy with central compartment dissection
Sistrunk procedure with removal of the central hyoid bone
items.explanation: A midline neck cyst that moves with tongue protrusion is a thyroglossal duct cyst, and the duct runs through or behind the hyoid. Cure requires the Sistrunk procedure, resecting the cyst, the tract, and the central hyoid body up to the foramen cecum, which lowers recurrence. Simple excision and sclerotherapy recur often, and thyroidectomy is not needed when normal thyroid tissue is present.

items.stem: A 35-year-old man with MEN2A has a 2.4 cm medullary thyroid carcinoma and a 4 cm left adrenal mass. Plasma metanephrines are elevated more than threefold, and he reports episodic headaches and palpitations. Which management sequence is most appropriate?
options: Alpha blockade, adrenalectomy first, then total thyroidectomy
Total thyroidectomy first, since the thyroid cancer is the larger threat
Both operations at the same time without preoperative blockade
Beta blockade alone, then thyroidectomy and observation of the adrenal
items.explanation: When pheochromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma coexist, the pheochromocytoma is treated first after adequate alpha-adrenergic blockade, because anesthesia and thyroid surgery can precipitate a lethal catecholamine crisis. Total thyroidectomy follows. Doing both operations at once without blockade is unsafe, and beta blockade given alone, before alpha blockade, can cause unopposed alpha stimulation and a hypertensive crisis.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman has a 2.2 cm thyroid nodule with normal thyrotropin. Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration shows atypia of undetermined significance (Bethesda category III). There are no suspicious ultrasound features and no family history of thyroid cancer. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Total thyroidectomy with prophylactic central neck dissection at once
Radioactive iodine ablation of the nodule
Repeat fine needle aspiration or molecular testing of the aspirate
Discharge from care with no further evaluation
items.explanation: Bethesda category III carries an intermediate malignancy risk, and the usual response is repeat aspiration or molecular testing, with diagnostic lobectomy if the result remains indeterminate or clinical features worry. Total thyroidectomy with neck dissection is overtreatment before a diagnosis, radioactive iodine is not used for a diagnostic problem, and discharge ignores a lesion with nontrivial cancer risk.

items.stem: A 78-year-old man has a hard, fixed neck mass that doubled in size over three weeks, with stridor on exertion. Biopsy shows undifferentiated spindle and giant cells that are negative for thyroglobulin, consistent with anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Imaging shows tracheal invasion and lung metastases. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Total thyroidectomy with a central neck dissection and tracheal resection
Radioactive iodine ablation followed by long-term thyroid suppression
Observation with repeat imaging in three months
Airway protection and a multidisciplinary palliative plan of systemic and radiation therapy
items.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is highly lethal, and with invasion of the trachea and distant metastases, the goal is palliation, with airway management, and systemic or radiation therapy including targeted agents when a mutation is found. Curative resection is not possible. Tumor cells lose iodine uptake, so radioactive iodine is useless, and observation risks airway loss.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has weight gain, wide purple striae, and glucose intolerance. Plasma ACTH is elevated, and a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test fails to suppress cortisol. Pituitary imaging is normal, and inferior petrosal sinus sampling shows no central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient. Which source is most likely?
options: Corticotroph adenoma of the pituitary, with the usual suppression
Ectopic ACTH from a bronchial or other neuroendocrine tumor
Cortisol-secreting adenoma of the adrenal cortex
Exogenous glucocorticoid use for an unrelated illness
items.explanation: A raised ACTH points to an ACTH-dependent source, and absent suppression with high-dose dexamethasone plus no petrosal sinus gradient argues against a pituitary adenoma, which usually partly suppresses and shows a gradient. Ectopic secretion, often from a bronchial carcinoid or small-cell tumor, fits. Adrenal adenomas and exogenous steroids give suppressed ACTH, so they do not match.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has a screening mammogram that shows a 9 mm oval, circumscribed mass. Targeted ultrasound shows an oval, parallel, circumscribed hypoechoic mass without suspicious features, and nothing is palpable. The radiologist assigns a BI-RADS category 3 assessment. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy with clip placement of the lesion now
Excisional biopsy after wire localization of the mass
Short-interval follow-up imaging at six months to confirm stability
Return to routine annual screening in twelve months
items.explanation: BI-RADS 3 means probably benign, with a malignancy risk of 2 percent or less, so short-interval imaging at six months, then continued follow-up for up to two years, is the accepted approach. Biopsy or excision subjects the patient to procedures for a lesion this unlikely to be cancer. Returning to annual screening skips the stability check that justifies the category, and growth would be missed for a full year.

items.stem: A 19-year-old woman has a mobile, rubbery, well-circumscribed 2.5 cm breast mass that has been stable for a year. Ultrasound shows an oval, circumscribed, hypoechoic mass, and ultrasound-guided core biopsy shows fibroadenoma, which the radiologist considers concordant. She has no family history of breast cancer. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Clinical observation, with excision reserved for growth or patient preference
Wide excision with a generous margin of normal breast tissue around the lesion
Mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy to be safe
Tamoxifen for six months to shrink the lesion
items.explanation: A concordant core biopsy diagnosis of fibroadenoma in a young woman is managed by observation, because the lesion is benign and often stable or regressing. Excision is offered for growth, symptoms, or preference, and giant or rapidly growing masses may need to be distinguished from phyllodes tumor. Mastectomy and sentinel node biopsy are far too aggressive, and tamoxifen does not treat a benign stromal-epithelial lesion.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman has had diffuse erythema, warmth, and peau d'orange skin involving over a third of the left breast for five weeks, with no response to antibiotics. A biopsy shows invasive ductal carcinoma with dermal lymphatic invasion. Staging shows no distant disease. What is the best initial treatment sequence?
options: Skin-sparing mastectomy with immediate implant reconstruction
Neoadjuvant systemic therapy, then mastectomy with axillary dissection and radiation
Lumpectomy with sentinel node biopsy and radiation
Immediate mastectomy followed by adjuvant chemotherapy
items.explanation: Inflammatory breast cancer is clinically staged as T4d and is treated with neoadjuvant systemic therapy first, followed by modified radical mastectomy with axillary dissection and postmastectomy radiation. Breast conservation, sentinel node biopsy, and skin-sparing mastectomy are not standard because of dermal lymphatic involvement, and immediate reconstruction is deferred. Starting with surgery before systemic therapy gives poorer outcomes.

items.stem: A 51-year-old man has a painless, firm, cystic 3 cm level II neck mass that has persisted for two months. Fine needle aspiration shows squamous cells, and testing for p16 is positive. Examination of the upper aerodigestive tract, including nasopharyngeal endoscopy, shows no primary tumor. Which is the best next step?
options: Modified radical neck dissection alone, with no search for the primary tumor
Excision of the cystic mass as an isolated branchial cyst
Radioactive iodine therapy to treat the cystic metastasis
Imaging, then tonsillectomy and tongue base biopsies to locate the primary
items.explanation: A cystic level II node with squamous cells that is p16 positive is the classic presentation of human papillomavirus related oropharyngeal cancer, and the primary often hides in the tonsil or tongue base crypts. After imaging, directed biopsies, tonsillectomy, or tongue base mucosectomy locate it in most cases. Treating it as a branchial cyst in an adult is a diagnostic error, and radioactive iodine treats thyroid cancer.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman with untreated Graves disease develops fever of 40 C, heart rate of 152, agitation, and vomiting after an emergency appendectomy. Thyroid storm is diagnosed. A beta blocker and supportive care have been started. Which additional drug should be given at least an hour after the thionamide?
options: Radioactive iodine by mouth, to destroy the overactive gland
Potassium iodide solution
A second thionamide dose given together with a calcium channel blocker
Intravenous levothyroxine to restore feedback inhibition of the gland
items.explanation: Iodide blocks thyroid hormone release, but if it is given before a thionamide has blocked new synthesis, it can supply substrate and worsen hormone production, so it follows the thionamide by about an hour. Radioactive iodine acts too slowly and is not used in an acute crisis. Levothyroxine would add hormone to a patient already in excess, and a calcium channel blocker is no substitute for a beta blocker.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman has had a scaly, red, weeping eruption of the right nipple and areola for four months. It has not improved with a topical corticosteroid. There is no palpable mass, and mammography is unremarkable. Which is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
options: Full-thickness punch biopsy of the nipple and areolar skin
Continued topical steroid therapy for a further three months
Culture of the skin surface and a course of oral antibiotics
Screening mammography again after one year of observation
items.explanation: A unilateral eczematous nipple lesion that does not heal with topical therapy is Paget disease of the nipple until a biopsy shows otherwise, and it is associated with underlying ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive cancer in most cases. A punch or wedge biopsy shows intraepidermal Paget cells. Prolonged steroids, antibiotics, and delayed imaging waste time, and a normal mammogram does not exclude the disease.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has a 2.5 cm squamous cell carcinoma of the lateral oral tongue with no clinically or radiologically palpable neck nodes. Depth of invasion is 8 mm. He is scheduled for wide local excision of the primary tumor. Which neck management is most appropriate?
options: No neck treatment, with observation by physical examination
Bilateral radical neck dissection of levels I to V
Level V dissection alone, because the posterior triangle is at highest risk
Elective ipsilateral selective neck dissection of levels I to III
items.explanation: Oral tongue cancers with a depth of invasion beyond about 4 mm carry a substantial risk of occult nodal disease, so elective ipsilateral selective neck dissection of levels I to III, extended to IV in some cases, is advised. Observation risks regional failure, and radical neck dissection is unnecessary in a clinically negative neck. Oral cavity tumors drain mainly to levels I to III, not V.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has amenorrhea for eight months and milky nipple discharge. She is not pregnant and takes no medications. Serum prolactin is 180 ng/mL, and magnetic resonance imaging shows an 8 mm pituitary microadenoma with no mass effect. Which is the appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Transsphenoidal resection of the pituitary tumor at once
External beam radiation to the sella turcica
A dopamine agonist such as cabergoline
A somatostatin analog given by monthly injection
items.explanation: Prolactinomas respond to dopamine agonists such as cabergoline, which normalize prolactin, shrink the tumor, and restore menses in most patients, so medical therapy is first line even for larger lesions. Transsphenoidal surgery is reserved for intolerance or resistance, and radiation is a later option because of slow effect and hypopituitarism risk. Somatostatin analogs are used mainly for growth hormone adenomas.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman who smokes has a tender, fluctuant mass beside the left areola for four days, with a history of two similar episodes in the same location that drained spontaneously. She is not lactating. Ultrasound confirms a 3 cm collection. Which is the best long-term plan after treating this episode?
options: Repeated needle aspiration with each recurrence of the abscess, with oral antibiotics
Excision of the involved duct system once inflammation has resolved
Lifelong prophylactic antibiotics taken daily for recurrence
Subcutaneous mastectomy with immediate implant reconstruction
items.explanation: Recurrent periareolar abscess in a nonlactating smoker reflects chronic subareolar duct inflammation and squamous metaplasia of the ducts, and it recurs unless the diseased duct system is excised after the acute episode settles. Repeated aspiration treats each flare but not the cause, prophylactic antibiotics do not alter duct anatomy, and mastectomy is out of proportion to a benign condition. Stopping smoking is advised alongside.

items.stem: A 2-year-old child has a marfanoid habitus, bumpy lips, and mucosal neuromas of the tongue, with chronic constipation due to intestinal ganglioneuromatosis. Testing shows a RET M918T variant, and serum calcitonin is mildly elevated. When should thyroidectomy be performed?
options: After puberty, when the gland has finished its growth
Only when a thyroid nodule becomes palpable on examination
At age 15 to 20 years, to allow normal development
As soon as the diagnosis is made, ideally in infancy
items.explanation: MEN2B with the RET M918T variant carries the highest risk, with medullary thyroid carcinoma that can appear in infancy and metastasize early, so prophylactic total thyroidectomy is advised in the first year of life or as soon as the diagnosis is made by an experienced surgeon. Waiting for a nodule or for puberty allows spread and lowers the chance of cure.

items.stem: During total thyroidectomy for a multinodular goiter, the surgeon examines the resected specimen and finds a small, tan, devascularized parathyroid gland attached to the capsule. The other three glands are viable. What should be done with the gland?
options: Confirm it by frozen section, mince it, and implant it in the sternocleidomastoid muscle
Discard it, since three viable glands will maintain normal calcium
Replace it unchanged beside the thyroid bed with a single suture
Send it for permanent section only and leave the wound open
items.explanation: A devascularized parathyroid gland that cannot be left in place is autotransplanted, after confirming it is parathyroid tissue, by mincing and implanting it into a muscle pocket such as the sternocleidomastoid, which preserves function and allows easy access later. Discarding it risks hypoparathyroidism, an unperfused gland sutured in place will not survive, and leaving the wound open does nothing for the gland.

items.stem: A 57-year-old woman has a clinically node-negative 2.3 cm invasive ductal carcinoma, hormone receptor positive and HER2 negative. She chooses lumpectomy and planned whole-breast radiation. Sentinel node biopsy shows metastases in two of three nodes, and no matting or extranodal extension is found. What is the appropriate axillary management?
options: Completion axillary node dissection to level III
Internal mammary node dissection to stage the disease
Completion axillary dissection is not required, and adjuvant therapy is planned
Repeat sentinel node biopsy at a later operation
items.explanation: In women with T1 or T2, clinically node-negative disease undergoing breast-conserving surgery with whole-breast radiation, one or two positive sentinel nodes do not require completion axillary dissection, because trials showed no survival or regional control difference. The radiation fields cover much of the lower axilla. Internal mammary dissection is not standard, and repeating sentinel biopsy would not alter management.

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman has a soft, nontender 4 cm cystic mass along the anterior border of the upper sternocleidomastoid muscle that enlarged after an upper respiratory infection. A second branchial cleft cyst is diagnosed. Which describes the course of its tract during excision?
options: Superficial to the facial nerve, ending in the external auditory canal
Posterior to the carotid sheath, ending at the pyriform sinus
Along the thyroid cartilage, ending at the foramen cecum
Between the internal and external carotid arteries toward the tonsillar fossa
items.explanation: A second branchial cleft anomaly tracks along the anterior sternocleidomastoid, passes between the internal and external carotid arteries, runs over the hypoglossal and glossopharyngeal nerves, and ends near the tonsillar fossa, so a full excision follows it up. A tract to the external auditory canal is characteristic of the first cleft, one to the pyriform sinus belongs to the fourth, and the foramen cecum marks the thyroglossal duct.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man on hemodialysis has bone pain, pruritus, and a parathyroid hormone level above 1,200 pg/mL despite phosphate binders, active vitamin D, and a calcimimetic. He has now developed painful skin necrosis from calciphylaxis. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Total parathyroidectomy with forearm autotransplantation
Focused excision of a single gland localized by sestamibi imaging
Increase of the dialysate calcium concentration and observation
Thyroid lobectomy with exploration of the central compartment
items.explanation: Secondary hyperparathyroidism from chronic kidney disease is diffuse hyperplasia of all glands, and failure of medical therapy with severe hyperparathyroidism or calciphylaxis is an indication for surgery. Subtotal parathyroidectomy or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation addresses every gland. A single-gland excision misses the hyperplasia, and raising dialysate calcium aggravates the vascular calcification, while thyroid surgery is irrelevant.

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has a 3.2 cm HER2-positive, estrogen receptor negative invasive ductal carcinoma with a biopsy-proven positive axillary node. Systemic staging is negative. She wants to preserve her breast if possible. Which approach is most appropriate to begin treatment?
options: Immediate mastectomy followed by endocrine therapy
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with HER2-directed therapy before surgery
Lumpectomy followed by observation of the axilla
Whole-breast radiation before any systemic treatment
items.explanation: Node-positive, HER2-positive disease responds well to neoadjuvant chemotherapy with HER2-targeted agents, which can shrink the tumor to permit breast conservation and shows prognostic information through pathologic complete response. Estrogen receptor negative disease has no benefit from endocrine therapy. Observation of a biopsy-proven positive axilla undertreats, and radiation alone before systemic therapy ignores the need for treating micrometastatic disease.

items.stem: Nine days after a tracheostomy in a ventilated patient, a small amount of bright red blood appears around the tube, then stops. Twenty minutes later there is brisk bleeding from the tube. The patient is hypotensive. What is the best next maneuver?
options: Transfer to radiology for urgent computed tomographic angiography
Packing of the stoma with gauze and later bronchoscopy
Digital pressure on the innominate artery against the sternum
Reduction of the tube cuff pressure to relieve mucosal ischemia
items.explanation: A sentinel bleed days after tracheostomy followed by brisk hemorrhage suggests a tracheoinnominate artery fistula, in which the tube tip or cuff erodes the artery. Overinflating the cuff, then finger compression of the artery against the posterior sternum through the stoma, buys time for operative repair. Imaging and gauze packing delay control, and deflating the cuff would remove tamponade.

items.stem: A 38-year-old premenopausal woman has a five-year invasive breast cancer risk of 4 percent by a validated risk model after a biopsy showing atypical lobular hyperplasia. She has an intact uterus and no history of thrombosis. She asks about medication to lower her risk. Which agent is most appropriate?
options: Tamoxifen, which is effective before and after menopause
Anastrozole, because aromatase inhibitors suit any age
Raloxifene, because it is the preferred premenopausal option
Low-dose oral estrogen to relieve the risk of atypia
items.explanation: Tamoxifen reduces breast cancer risk in high-risk women of any menopausal status. Aromatase inhibitors work only when ovarian estrogen production has stopped, so they are reserved for postmenopausal women. Raloxifene is approved only after menopause. Estrogen is not a preventive agent and may raise risk. Tamoxifen carries risks of thromboembolism and endometrial cancer, which is why a history of thrombosis would change the choice.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman has a 1.8 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma on needle biopsy and a 1.5 cm firm, level IV lymph node in the right lateral neck that is positive for papillary carcinoma on aspiration. The contralateral neck is normal on ultrasound. Which is the most appropriate operation?
options: Right thyroid lobectomy alone with observation of the nodes
Total thyroidectomy alone, leaving the lateral nodes for radioactive iodine
Bilateral radical neck dissection with sacrifice of the accessory nerve
Total thyroidectomy with central and right selective lateral neck dissection
items.explanation: Biopsy-proven lateral neck nodal metastasis from papillary cancer warrants therapeutic compartment-oriented dissection of the involved levels, usually II to V, along with total thyroidectomy and central dissection. Lobectomy alone leaves known nodal disease behind. Radioactive iodine is not a substitute for removing clinically evident nodes, and a bilateral radical dissection is unnecessary when the contralateral neck is clear.

items.stem: A 14-year-old boy has a firm, tender, 2 cm subareolar swelling in the left breast for two months. He is otherwise healthy, takes no medications, and has normal genital examination and Tanner stage 3 development. There is no skin change or nipple discharge. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate subcutaneous mastectomy through a periareolar incision
Ultrasound-guided core biopsy of the subareolar tissue
Reassurance and re-examination, since pubertal gynecomastia usually regresses
Measurement of tumor markers and a chest computed tomogram
items.explanation: Transient pubertal gynecomastia affects many adolescent boys and usually resolves within one to two years as hormones equilibrate, so a history and examination followed by observation is correct when no cause is found. Surgery is reserved for persistent, bothersome, or large cases. Biopsy and extensive laboratory or imaging work-up are unnecessary without atypical features such as a hard, eccentric mass.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman with long-standing Hashimoto thyroiditis has had a rapidly enlarging neck mass for six weeks with hoarseness and mild dyspnea. Ultrasound shows a diffusely enlarged, heterogeneous, hypoechoic gland. Fine needle aspiration is inconclusive. Which is the best next step?
options: Immediate total thyroidectomy with bilateral neck dissection
Core needle biopsy with flow cytometry to look for lymphoma
Radioactive iodine therapy for presumed papillary cancer
Increase of thyroid hormone replacement to shrink the gland
items.explanation: A rapidly growing goiter in a patient with Hashimoto thyroiditis suggests primary thyroid lymphoma, usually B-cell, and tissue with immunophenotyping is needed because aspiration alone is often nondiagnostic. Treatment is chemotherapy with radiation rather than extensive surgery. Radioactive iodine does not treat lymphoma, and increasing hormone replacement would not shrink a malignant process and delays diagnosis.
